seen: One row per decade of the seasonal transform: a yearly wave, about eleven per row, with a fast fuzz riding on it. The fuzz is thicker in some rows and thinner in others (rows 2, 4, 6 look thinner in their second halves). Nameable at once: a beat, every year, and a fuzz that swells and shrinks. That the beat is yearly needs the caption; that it repeats does not.

The same yearly beat as V20, but the rank scale has pushed the line against the top and bottom of each row: flat plateaus, a blocky square-ish wave, and the thin/thick contrast between rows made far starker than in V20. It looks clipped, but N0.3 is not quite it: nothing is cut off. What is wrong is that the contrast is the scale's, not the material's. No norm I hold said that, so N2 is written now.

Raw values, rank scale, one row per decade. Each row sits at a different height inside its band: high in the 1970s, falling through the 1990s, low in the 2000s, and the 2020s hugging the floor. That is the slow story of the day's length (my belief L1, recognised, not encountered). But the eye has to reassemble it across seven rows: the layout cuts one slow arc into seven segments. The yearly beat is there too, weaker. Failure is the cut, not the scale; N2 also applies, less. N3 written now.

Strip, tidal, linear: a woven cloth of blue and red with diagonal hatching. At first look a texture, so N0.1 fails it. A second look found what the first did not: pale horizontal bands where the hatching nearly vanishes, recurring down the page at roughly equal spacing (around rows 7-9, 17-19, 27-29 counted by eye; not measured). That is not on my list of beliefs (L3 names tidal terms, not a slow swelling of them). The diagonals I cannot tell apart from a beat between the tidal period and the calendar grid (N0.2). Fails at thirty seconds; the bands are kept as a note for V20's thick and thin rows, which may be the same thing.

V19 with a linear scale. The amplitudes are now honest (N2 is satisfied) and the slow story is almost gone: each row's height inside its band shifts by a little, the 1990s row visibly sinks, and nothing else of the decadal arc reads. The yearly beat and the fast fuzz show, quieter than V20. Fails on N3, written two variants ago: the slow movement is cut into seven pieces, and here the pieces are too small even to reassemble.

Strip, seasonal, rank. One shape at once: a dark blue column down the middle of every year (roughly days 150-250 by the pixel position, so northern summer), red on both sides, the red split into two lobes. Recognition of L2 (the seasonal cycle), and the two lobes look like the semi-annual term. Two norms speak against it and I overrule both. N0.4: nothing tells a stranger which way time runs, but the shape does not need time's direction, only the year's. N2: the rank scale sharpens the edge of the blue column, but it does not make the column; the place of the shape is the material's even if its contrast is the scale's. N4 written now to say where N2 stops.

V10 with a rank scale: the same woven cloth, more saturated, and the pale bands that V10's second look found are mostly gone. Rank flattened the swelling of the tidal amplitude, which is the only shape V10 had. A texture at thirty seconds (N0.1), and N2 in its plain sense: the scale erased the material's amplitude.

Spiral, seasonal, linear: a disc, blue in its lower half (the summer side, since January stands at twelve o'clock), red above. The seasonal shape is there. But the first thing the eye takes is optical: moire rings and spokes near the centre, and a seam running straight up from the hole where each year joins the next. That is the renderer's structure competing with the material's (N0.2). And the outer years look paler than the inner ones only because their dots are spread over a longer circumference: the layout gives later years more room and less ink. No norm said that; N5 written now, not decisive here.

Line, tidal, linear, the whole sixty-four years left to right. It looks like the waveform of a sound: a dark mass that swells and narrows, four swells across the width, the narrow waists at roughly a third, a half-and-a-bit and four fifths of the way along (by eye). A stranger says 'it breathes' within seconds. This is the thing V10's pale bands and V20's thick and thin rows were glimpses of: the size of the fast tidal wobble itself swells and shrinks on a period of very roughly eighteen or nineteen years, by eye. Not on my list of beliefs. An encounter, and it arrived at a variant made by a grid, not by a decision.

Spiral, raw, rank. A red heart and a blue rim, like the cross-section of a trunk: the early years (inside) long days, the recent years (outside) short. The slow story reads in one radial sweep, so N3 is met where V18 and V19 failed it, and N4 admits the rank scale because the colour's place is what matters. N0.1 says it works. But N5, written one variant ago, says what is wrong: the rim, which is the recent and most surprising part (the shortest days), is drawn in sparse dots and looks faint, while the heart is dense. The two norms pull apart and I cannot decide. Unsure, held back by N5.

Strip, raw, linear. Horizontal bands: deep red across the upper third, a pale band, red again, then blue down to a dark blue floor in the last rows; a faint lighter column in mid-year behind it. The slow story reads in one downward sweep (N3 met), every year gets the same ink (N5 met), and N0.1 says works. It is the clearest picture of the slow movement so far, and I wanted to pass it. N0.4 stops it, and here it bites where at V09 I overruled it: V09's shape was a season and did not need time's direction; this shape is a trend and does. Nothing on the page says whether red is the past or the future. A prior norm decided against my liking.

V04 with a rank scale. The four swells are still there, but the mass now fills the frame from edge to edge and the waists are shallow. What V04 showed is an amplitude, the size of the wobble growing and shrinking, and rank is the one scale that flattens amplitude. N2, written at V21, decides it in its plain sense.

V06 with a rank scale: the same bands, red above and blue below, more saturated. N4 admits the rank scale, since what is read is where the colour changes. It fails where V06 failed, and for the same reason: a trend with no direction on the page. Judged by the same norm in the same way; I note that consistency here is cheap, because the two images differ only in saturation.

V13 with a linear scale: the red heart, and the rim almost gone into the paper. Where V13 left me unsure, this one decides: the recent years, which carry the shortest days, are the faintest part of the image only because the spiral spreads them thin. N5. A note on the practice rather than the variant: this is the third spiral, and it taught nothing the first two had not. Once a layout's defect is structural, the remaining cells of the grid in that layout are what Iteration, not Imitation calls variation without concretization.

Line, seasonal, rank, sixty-four years in 1,040 pixels. Each year is one stroke, so the page is a comb or a barcode, top to bottom, and the dark clusters inside it (the fast terms, and faintly the four swells of V04) sit behind the comb. A stranger names 'stripes', which is the pixel budget, not the material. N0.1: a texture. N2 too, rank stretching every year to full height.

Line, seasonal, linear. A waveform again; the yearly strokes form a comb as in V03, but with honest amplitudes, and the four swells of V04 show through, fainter. Taken alone, N0.1 would pass it: 'it breathes' can be said. I fail it because V04 says the same thing louder, and I am judging it beside V04, not alone. None of N0 or N1-N5 says a variant is judged against the others. N6 written now: the grid has turned the verdict comparative.

Strip, seasonal, linear: V09 with honest contrast. The blue summer column is there, softer, inside the same woven hatching. By N0.1 alone it would work, as V09 did. N6, written one variant ago, fails it, because V09 shows the column more clearly. This verdict depends on the viewing order: V09 came sixth and V08 seventeenth. Had the seed put V08 first, N6 would have failed V09 instead, or (more likely) never been written at V02. The order was not mine, and it is deciding.

Line, raw, rank. The slow story in one stroke, left to right: up to a long high plateau, a fall, a second smaller high, a cliff, a low stretch, a rise, and the last years at the floor. Uncut (N3), the direction given by the ordinary convention of a line read left to right (N0.4), nameable as 'it fell, came back, and fell lower'. Rank stretches the heights, which N2 forbids where the eye reads amplitude; I let N4 admit it because the reading is of order (higher, lower, lowest), not of how much. That is a fine line, and I drew it in this variant's favour.

Decades, tidal, rank. Every row is filled edge to edge with a fast regular oscillation; in the second halves of rows 2, 4 and 6 it goes ragged. The ragged stretches are where V04's waists fall: there the tidal wobble is smallest, and the rank scale has stretched what is left (other terms, noise) to the full height. So the swell V04 showed as size is shown here as tidiness, which a stranger cannot read as size. N2. N6 as well, beside V04.

Spiral, tidal, linear: a speckled disc of red and blue dots, finer at the centre, sparse at the rim, with faint spokes. Nothing to point at. N0.1, a texture. I looked for the swells as rings of pale and found none I would swear to.

V16 with a rank scale: the same speckled disc, more saturated, a faint radial spoke pattern more visible. A texture (N0.1); the spokes are the renderer's (N0.2). The fourth spiral that fails for reasons the first one already gave.

Line, raw, linear: the grid's first cell, seen twenty-second. The slow story as V01 told it, with honest heights: a rise to a high early peak, a long fall, a smaller second hump, a cliff, a low trough, a modest recovery, and the last years lowest of all, with the fast fuzz riding on top throughout. Nameable at once, uncut, directed, and N2 is met without help from N4.

A revision, written beside the original and not in place of it. At V01 I let N4 admit a rank scale on a reading I called 'of order, not of how much', and said I drew that line in V01's favour. V00 shows the same story with honest heights at least as clearly, so the favour was not needed: N6 now fails V01, and N2 in its plain sense with it. The original verdict stands in line 18 as it was given.

Spiral, seasonal, rank: the spiral's best cell. The blue sector sits at the bottom and lower left of a clock face whose twelve o'clock is New Year, red above and to the right. Here the layout fits the material: a year is a circle, and the strip of V09 cuts it at December. That is a real advantage and no norm of mine names it. But the moire and the seam are still the first thing seen (N0.2, weaker than in V14), and V09 shows the summer more clearly. N6 decides. A norm for the circle's advantage would have been minted only to rescue this cell, and I do not write it.

Decades, tidal, linear: the fast wobble with honest heights, and within each row it visibly grows and shrinks (row 2 shrinks to the right, row 3 grows, row 4 shrinks). The swell is there, but it is longer than a decade, so every row holds only part of one, and the eye has to carry it from row end to row start. N3, written for the slow arc of the day's length at V19, now decides a different slow movement, the swell; I applied it without rewriting it. N6 too, beside V04.

The norms as a mould: one black ribbon, 1962 to 2026, its centre the year-averaged length of day, its thickness the size of the fast wobble. The slow story is the clearest of the night: rise, high plateau, fall, a second hump, the trough, a rise, and the steepest fall at the end. But the ribbon's thickness hardly changes. The swell V04 showed is a few tenths of a millisecond on a page scaled to several milliseconds; N2 kept the scale honest and so the swell went under. The variant was built to meet N1, and N1 fails it. Two norms of my own collide in the form they were meant to produce. N7 written now, to settle the collision; so the norm list was not closed after twenty-four variants.
